summary: A proposal defining a data compression mode for the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol, which RFC 454 had called HASP mode and promised to define later. The author explains the aim of saving network bandwidth on large file transfers, such as those expected for big machines joining the network.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to shrink files before sending them, like packing a suitcase tighter, so the shipment takes less room on the network.

subtitle: A data compression scheme for efficient large file transfers in FTP

tldr.problem: FTP was designed for efficient large file transfers, but as big computers like Illiac IV join the ARPANET, bandwidth costs become a concern. RFC 454 promised a compression mode called HASP but did not define it.
tldr.mechanism: Bob Braden proposes a simple linear compression scheme adapted from IBM's HASP system. It encodes repeated characters and runs of filler bytes efficiently, using small descriptor fields to mark whether bytes are raw data, repetitions, or filler.
tldr.outcome: The scheme was not widely adopted; modern FTP implementations rely on external compression tools instead. However, the RFC's economics analysis—comparing CPU cost to compress against transmission savings—influenced later thinking about protocol design.

today: RFC 468 proposed an in-FTP compression mode, but the approach was not standardized. Modern FTP implementations typically rely on external compression tools or use compression at the transport layer. However, the RFC's analysis of compression economics—weighing CPU cost against bandwidth savings—remains a foundational principle in network protocol design.

sections.title: The Need for Compression
sections.content: Bob Braden at UCLA explains that as the ARPANET grows and facilities like Illiac IV join, users will need to send enormous amounts of data—one user expected to transmit 200 million bits per day. FTP was designed for efficiency, and RFC 454 promised a compression mode, but never defined it. This RFC delivers the promised definition. Braden notes that compression is particularly effective for printer files from remote job entry, where real deployments showed compression ratios of two to three times.
sections.plainLanguage: Early ARPANET computers needed to send huge files. Sending smaller, squeezed versions would save bandwidth and money, so FTP promised a compression mode—this is the definition.

sections.title: The Compression Scheme
sections.content:
The compression method is simple and linear—CPU time is proportional to the input size. It uses a descriptor byte to mark what follows: a flag of zero introduces raw data bytes, a flag of 10 (binary) means n repetitions of a single byte, 11 means n filler bytes (spaces for text, zeros for binary), and a special all-zero byte marks end-of-record. The count field and the byte size are variable, with the RFC allowing different byte sizes.

For example, a run of ten spaces in a text file would be encoded as a short two-byte descriptor (flag 11 and count 10) instead of ten literal spaces. Repetitions of any character work the same way. This is effective for text files with repeated characters and whitespace.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending ten blanks, send one code that means 'ten blanks'. For any character that repeats, send a code instead.

sections.title: Economics of Compression
sections.content: Braden analyzes whether compression is worth the CPU time. His estimate for 1973 hardware is that a simple linear compression algorithm costs about 5 cents per megabit in CPU cycles, while transmitting the same megabit costs over 30 cents (and the author expects it to rise). Therefore, spending CPU cycles to reduce bandwidth is economical, and the advantage will only grow as bandwidth costs remain higher than CPU costs. He dismisses more complex (quadratic) compression schemes because their CPU overhead quickly exceeds savings.
sections.plainLanguage: Squishing a file (using CPU) costs 5 cents per megabit. Sending it (using the network) costs 30+ cents. So compression saves money.

sections.title: The HASP Origin
sections.content: Braden includes background on IBM's HASP system (Houston Automatic Spooling Program), a job-spooling and batch processing system that became widely used on large IBM 360 computers. HASP includes its own compression scheme as part of its Multileaving Protocol for remote batch entry. The RFC's compression design adapts HASP's proven scheme to FTP's needs, though it changes some details for better efficiency in the network context. Braden notes HASP's cultural significance among IBM users and its influence on a generation of systems programmers.
sections.plainLanguage: IBM's HASP was a famous system for managing batch jobs, and it had its own compression scheme. This RFC borrows from HASP's proven design.

references.text: Braden, R. T., "Interim NETRJS Specifications", RFC 189, July 1971.
